Neonates of the Eastern coral snake emerge from their parchment-shelled eggs after an incubation period of approximately 49 days [ab = approximately 49 days] when maintained at a constant 23 °C [T = 23 °C], a duration that falls slightly below the typical range of 78 to 93 days reported for this species under natural thermal regimes. At hatching, the young measure roughly 20.25 cm [Lb = roughly 20.25 cm] in total length, a size that positions them among the larger neonates relative to body-proportioned elapids. This initial length is complemented by a modest birth weight of 2.3 grams [Wwb = 2.3 grams], a mass derived from the dimensions of the egg, which itself averages 3.34 cm in length and 1.15 cm in width. The leathery-shelled egg thus provides a finite yolk reserve that sustains the lecithotrophic embryo through its entire development, and the resulting hatchling is fully capable of independent locomotion and prey capture from the moment of eclosion. This pattern of relatively brief incubation coupled with a substantial neonatal size reflects an adaptive compromise between the risks of prolonged egg exposure in humid subtropical environments and the advantages of producing offspring large enough to subdue small fossorial prey immediately.

Sexual maturation in the Eastern coral snake is tightly linked to body size rather than strictly to age, a pattern common among elapids in which reproductive activation is gated by somatic growth. Females typically attain puberty at a total length of 43.18 cm [Lp = 43.18 cm], whereas males reach this milestone at a slightly smaller size of 40.2 cm [Lp = 40.2 cm]. This dimorphism in maturation thresholds mirrors the ultimate size divergence between the sexes, as adult females achieve a substantially greater maximum total length of 112.4 cm [Li = 112.4 cm], nearly double the 68.5 cm [Li = 68.5 cm] recorded for fully grown males. The physiological trigger for gonadal activation appears to be achievement of a critical mass threshold rather than a fixed chronological age; field-captured juveniles exhibit no evidence of gametogenesis until these length benchmarks are surpassed. This size-based reproductive strategy likely reflects the constraints imposed by a venomous, slow-moving foraging mode, where larger body size confers advantages in prey handling and energy storage for vitellogenesis.

Body mass increases predictably with snout–vent length in this species, as documented by direct measurements from field-collected specimens. At a snout–vent length of 55.1 cm, individuals weigh approximately 30.1 grams , and at 59.6 cm SVL, the recorded mass rises to 33.3 grams . These weight-for-length data points illustrate a relatively linear relationship between size and mass in the sub-adult to adult size range, suggesting that body condition indices in Micrurus fulvius are fairly stable across intermediate body sizes. The modest weight gain of roughly 3.2 grams over a 4.5 cm increase in SVL implies that these snakes devote a significant portion of their energetic intake to linear growth rather than to surplus fat storage during their pre-reproductive years. This physiological strategy aligns with the species' habit of consuming elongated, low-energy-density prey such as other snakes and amphisbaenians, which may limit the rate at which energy reserves can be accumulated.

Reproductive output in the Eastern coral snake is modest in comparison to many sympatric colubrids, reflecting the constraints imposed by its venomous, sit-and-wait foraging ecology. At a snout–vent length of 136.7 cm, a gravid female produces a maximum of 12 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 12 eggs per clutch], and typically deposits only one clutch each year [F_R_i = one clutch each year]. This low annual fecundity is compensated by a relatively high investment per offspring, as evidenced by the dimensions of the egg. The species' reproductive rate is thus realized through infrequent, moderately sized clutches rather than through frequent, small batches of eggs. This pattern is consistent with the broader elapid tendency toward extended inter-brood intervals, likely driven by the energetic costs of yolk production in a snake that relies on infrequent, large meals. The combination of a single annual clutch and a moderate clutch size places Micrurus fulvius at the slow end of the life-history continuum among New World elapids.

Longevity records for the Eastern coral snake indicate a remarkable capacity for extended survival under captive conditions. The maximum lifespan documented for this species, 19 years [am = 19 years], was recorded in an individual maintained at a constant environmental temperature of 23 °C [T = 23 °C]. This exceptional longevity is noteworthy for a relatively small-bodied elapid and likely reflects a slow metabolic pace, a low intrinsic mortality rate in the absence of predation, and the absence of the high energetic costs associated with frequent reproduction. In nature, however, realized lifespans are presumably far shorter due to predation by ophiophagous raptors, larger snakes, and mammalian carnivores, as well as the risks of seasonal temperature extremes in the pine flatwoods and hardwood hammocks it inhabits. The stark contrast between captive and wild longevity underscores the role of extrinsic mortality in shaping the life-history evolution of this species, favoring a strategy of delayed maturation and infrequent, high-investment reproduction over a potentially extended reproductive window.
